Abstract

The emergence of various topological semimetal states presents a novel opportunity for enhancing the efficiency of thermoelectric transport. This study introduces a recipe to improve the thermoelectric (TE) performance in topological materials containing single-pair Weyl points (SP WPs) fermions and phonons. The recipe focuses on two key factors contributing to the enhancement of TE performance: the increase in the density of states to achieve a high power factor, and the introduction of additional phonon scattering to reduce the lattice thermal conductivity. The proposed recipe is confirmed in a half-metallic SP WPs material BaNiIO6 through first-principles methods. An enhanced density of states arises near the energy of the SP WPs in BaNiIO6, leading to a peak power factor connected to the complex Fermi surface due to the degeneracy of Weyl pockets in energy. Furthermore, it is shown that the SP WPs phonons in BaNiIO6 possess a high scattering rate and can likely contribute to the low lattice thermal conductivity, especially when two crossing points in SP WPs do not degenerate in frequency. The new recipe can be used for discovering high-performance thermoelectric materials in the future by utilizing the transport advantages of degenerate-in-energy SP WPs fermions and non-degenerate-in-frequency SP WPs phonons.

1 Introduction

The discovery of high-performance thermoelectric (TE) materials[1-3] for cooling or power generation remains a significant challenge in physics and material science. Examples of traditional TE materials,[4-9] such as PbTe, Bi2Te3, CoSb3, and SnSe, which often possess high power factor and low lattice thermal conductivity with the optimal zT can be tuned to exceed 1 under room temperature. However, if we want to realize 10% conversion efficiency of the TE device, the zT should be greater than 2.[10] The dimensionless figure of merit zT of TE materials is given by zT = S2σT/κ, where S is the Seebeck coefficient, σ is the electrical conductivity, T is the absolute temperature, and κ is the thermal conductivity including electronic (κe) and lattice contributions (κl). Owing to the opposite dependence on carrier density, it is challenging to improve S and σ simultaneously to enlarge the power factor, PF = S2σ. Afterward, many strategies, including band degeneracy and quantum confinement, are developed to enhance PF, which allows the increase of S without overshadowing σ.[11-18] According to the Motto relation, S is much improved when the density of states (DOS) is a rapidly varying function of energy.[19] The size-quantization effect does this in low-dimensional structures; the sharp maxima in DOS can result in a substantial increase in S and, thereby, the PF. Another strategy for improving zT focuses on reducing κl by introducing nanostructures to bulk, which allows for diverse phonon scattering.[20-23] For example, introducing PbS nanoparticles to PbTe leads to a 60% decrease of κl.[24]
